title: Vivekananda Greets Chicago as Family
text:
In September 1893 the World's Parliament of Religions opened in Chicago, alongside the great World's Columbian Exposition. Speakers from many faiths gathered before an audience of several thousand. Among them was a young Hindu monk from India, Swami Vivekananda, almost unknown in America, who had arrived with little money and no official delegation behind him.

On the opening day, September 11, he had postponed his turn several times out of nervousness. When he finally rose in his orange robe and turban, he began with the words "Sisters and Brothers of America." Before he could go on, the audience rose to its feet and applauded for a long time.

His short speech that followed spoke of tolerance and universal acceptance. He said he was proud to belong to a religion that had sheltered persecuted refugees of other faiths, and quoted a Hindu hymn comparing the different paths people take to streams that all flow into the same sea.

Newspapers described him as one of the most impressive figures at the Parliament. He spent the next years lecturing in America and Britain and became one of the first teachers to bring Hindu philosophy to a broad Western audience.
lesson: Speak to strangers as members of your own family, and they often respond in kind. Warmth that comes before argument opens doors argument alone cannot.
source: John Henry Barrows, ed., The World's Parliament of Religions (1893); The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1
